title: Sh2-82, Cocoon Nebula
caption: The Cocoon Nebula (Sh2-82), imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
credit: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage) and H. Schweiker (WIYN and NOIRLab/NSF/AURA)

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: A small red glow sits inside a blue haze, and a long lane of dust cuts diagonally across the frame. This is Sh2-82 in the constellation Sagitta, which is informally known as both the Cocoon Nebula and the 'little Trifid Nebula'.

Sh2-82 is a fairly small emission nebula, the red part, surrounded by a blue reflection nebula. The two kinds of nebula shine for different reasons. An emission nebula glows because hot stars energize its gas, while a reflection nebula shines by starlight bouncing off dust grains, which scatter blue light most readily.

The dark diagonal dust lane hides most of the stars that lie beyond it, which is why the star field looks thinner along its path. Dust like this is common in star-forming regions of our galaxy, where it both hides and helps build new stars.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope used four filters. B is shown in blue, V in green, I in orange and hydrogen-alpha in red.
